Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $\chi^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ensemble null tests that use multivariate distribution comparisons to detect subtle systematic errors that traditional scalar statistics often miss.
AI.motivation: Standard systematic error checks, such as averaging measurements or using $\chi^2$ tests, can hide important structural information, allowing unrecognized errors to undermine scientific discoveries.
AI.method: The authors propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions of experimental data against reference distributions obtained from observations or simulations.
AI.result: The method successfully detected systematic effects in CMB simulations missed by $\chi^2$ tests, identified velocity asymmetry in Gaia data, and exposed control mismatches in CRISPR screens.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble testing transforms repeated measurements into a powerful tool for discovering 'unknown unknowns,' providing a more robust empirical foundation for large-scale scientific datasets.

title: Latent Prediction Yields Cross-Subject Alignable Representations in Sensory-Evoked fMRI
summary: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a central analytical tool in cognitive neuroscience. Here we ask whether self-supervised learning (SSL), which has been scarcely explored in this domain, can yield representations that support strong downstream performance. To do so, we adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on brain data alone. The encoders never see the stimulus images or any representation derived from them. Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) using a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) can learn robust brain representations from fMRI data without ever seeing the original stimuli.
AI.motivation: Traditional fMRI decoding models rely on supervised learning, requiring paired stimulus-brain data. This limits scalability and prevents the pooling of data across different participants or datasets.
AI.method: The researchers adapted a JEPA framework to train participant-specific encoders using only brain activity (Natural Scenes Dataset). Crucially, the model has no access to the images or language labels during the pre-training phase.
AI.result:
1. **Competitive Performance**: The SSL encoders match supervised models in brain captioning and image reconstruction tasks.
2. **Unsupervised Alignment**: Encoders from different participants can be aligned without using shared stimuli or images.
3. **Zero-shot Generalization**: Once aligned, a decoding head trained on one participant works on another with minimal performance loss.
AI.conclusion: This approach enables the scaling of fMRI analysis by allowing researchers to pool data across individuals and datasets without the need for perfectly matched experimental stimuli, moving closer to a universal brain decoder.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: this https URL

AI.tldr: The study identifies that LLM-brain alignment is driven by a small, compact subspace (1-3% of dimensions) that is distinct from the principal components of variance within the model.
AI.motivation: To understand which specific components of LLM representations drive alignment with neural activity and how these components relate to the model's internal variance.
AI.method: Ridge reduced-rank regression to identify brain-predictive subspaces across three naturalistic datasets and six model conditions, comparing results with Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
AI.result: Neural predictivity is concentrated in a low-dimensional, compact subspace that generalizes across participants and datasets, and these directions are distinct from the axes of maximum variance in LLM embeddings.
AI.conclusion: LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of representations, providing a framework to understand why specific model features align with neural activity.

title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
summary: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

AI.tldr: ClinGeX is an LLM agent with 105 executable skills that outperforms existing methods in clinical genomic analysis, enhancing both accuracy and speed in human-AI collaboration.
AI.motivation: The increasing accessibility of sequencing has made clinical genomic analysis—which requires integrating evolving guidelines and databases—a major bottleneck in clinical decision-making due to its complexity and labor-intensive nature.
AI.method: Developed ClinGeX, an LLM agent that utilizes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration, evaluated via benchmark cases and human-AI collaboration studies.
AI.result: ClinGeX achieved 71.7% macro-averaged task-level concordance on benchmarks, significantly outperforming the strongest comparator. In human studies, it increased case-level concordance across various medical domains and reduced interpretation time.
AI.conclusion: ClinGeX demonstrates that using executable domain-specific skills within an LLM agent framework significantly improves accuracy and efficiency in clinical genomic interpretation, supporting human-AI collaboration in real-world scenarios.

title: Hyaluronic acid over-expression drives tissue architecture in both healthy and diseased states
summary: Tissue architecture is shaped by a variety of biomechanical and biochemical mechanisms, including morphogen patterning, differential growth, and spatial variations in cellular contractility. These mechanisms typically emphasize forces generated within cells. Here, we explore a complementary mechanism in which intercellular space itself exerts forces that shape tissue architecture. More specifically, we focus on hyaluronic acid (HA), a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, that draws fluid into the spaces between cells through osmotic pressure, allowing these spaces to expand and mechanically deform the surrounding tissue. We propose that spatial patterning of HA-mediated extracellular forces, acting together with tissue geometry and junctional mechanics, provides a common physical framework capable of generating distinct tissue architectures. We test this hypothesis using a computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues to a flow network representing HA and extracellular fluid in the extracellular space. This coupled model demonstrates a range of architectural responses spanning changes in tissue topology and morphology: global HA overexpression drives fluid accumulation and cell-cell junction rupture to produce multiple lumens in nontrivial patterns; a localized HA-rich region generates pressure gradients that drive budding; {\it multiple localized HA-rich regions generate branching;} and {\it extended HA-rich patterns can drive tubular structures.} Our results have direct experimental implications and establish the spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces as a mechanical morphogen helping shape tissue architecture.

AI.tldr: Spatial patterning of hyaluronic acid (HA) in the extracellular space creates osmotic pressure that acts as a mechanical morphogen to shape tissue architecture, including lumen formation, budding, branching, and tubulogenesis.
AI.motivation: Traditional tissue morphogenesis models focus on forces generated within cells, overlooking the potential role of forces exerted by the intercellular space itself via osmotic pressure.
AI.method: A computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues with a flow network representing hyaluronic acid and extracellular fluid.
AI.result: Spatial patterning of HA-mediated forces can drive diverse morphological changes: fluid accumulation and junction rupture for multiple lumens, pressure gradients for budding, and extended patterns for branching and tubular structures.
AI.conclusion: HA-mediated intercellular forces serve as a mechanical morphogen that works alongside tissue geometry and junctional mechanics to shape tissue architecture.
